record.title: China’s CAC reports platform action against AI impersonation of public figures
record.summary: China’s Cyberspace Administration reported on 6 November that platforms had cleared more than 47,000 items and handled 3,961 accounts in cases involving AI-enabled impersonation of public figures. The notice describes deceptive commerce, fabricated rumors, follower acquisition and synthetic depictions. These are regulator-reported totals without a stated period or denominator; the notice does not establish effectiveness, reduced prevalence, independent verification or a new technical requirement.

claims.label: DEMONSTRATED
claims.text: China’s Cyberspace Administration published a notice on 6 November 2026 describing enforcement against AI-enabled impersonation of public figures for misleading commerce, rumor creation, follower acquisition and other promotion.

claims.label: CLAIMED
claims.text: The CAC notice states that platforms cleared more than 47,000 items and handled 3,961 accounts in the described enforcement. The notice supplies no reporting interval or denominator, and the totals have not been independently audited.

claims.label: NOT_ESTABLISHED
claims.text: The notice does not establish the prevalence of AI impersonation, the fraction of relevant conduct removed, implementation consistency across platforms, a reduction in harm, or a new binding technical requirement.

evidence_gaps.description: The report gives aggregate counts without a defined period or denominator, limiting interpretation of enforcement scale.
The counts and implementation are regulator-reported and not independently audited; no baseline or prevalence outcome is given.

brief.importance_rationale: If the regulator-reported totals reflect the described enforcement, the report gives a concrete but unaudited signal of platform action against AI impersonation used for deceptive promotion and misinformation. It does not measure prevalence reduction or establish a new technical control.
limitations: Counts are reported by the regulator and have no stated reporting interval or denominator.
The notice does not provide an independent audit, baseline, platform-level implementation details or measured reduction in impersonation.
This is an enforcement report, not evidence of a new binding AI rule or proven platform effectiveness.

technical.claimed_result: The CAC states that platforms cleared more than 47,000 items and handled 3,961 accounts in the described AI-enabled impersonation cases.
technical.demonstrated_result: The accessible official Chinese notice establishes that CAC published the report and described the actions; its administrative totals remain unaudited claims.
technical.mechanism: The notice says CAC urged platforms to conduct a concentrated clean-up, remove unlawful or non-compliant content and accounts, and strengthen platform responsibility. It provides examples but no detailed technical control or audit protocol.
technical.regime: One CAC notice published 6 November 2026 about AI-enabled imitation of public figures used for misleading commerce, rumor creation, follower acquisition and synthetic depictions. The reporting interval and denominator are not stated.
technical.reproducibility: No independent audit or corroborating platform-level dataset was located in this activation.
technical.strongest_baseline: No baseline, denominator, reporting interval or before/after prevalence measure is provided.

brief.title: China’s CAC reports platform action against AI impersonation of public figures
brief.why_it_matters: The notice offers a recent, concrete enforcement signal about AI-generated likeness and voice misuse. Its aggregate figures can inform monitoring of platform responses, but without a period, denominator, audit or baseline they do not show how common the conduct is or whether enforcement reduced it.

other.title: China's CAC announces a two-month campaign against misleading military content, including AI-generated fabrications
other.summary: A Chinese-language notice dated October 12 and published by the Cyberspace Administration of China on October 15 announces a two-month, multi-agency campaign against improper marketing and sensationalized military-related content online. The ten listed categories include AI-generated fake military dramas, stories and videos. The notice directs authorities to require platform review and cleanup, but reports no implementation results, AI-specific technical requirements or measured effects.
